props.title: Martin
props.initialSlug: Romero's unique take on vampire mythology

sections.content: George Romero's Martin revolutionized vampire cinema by stripping away supernatural elements and diving deep into psychological horror. Unlike the gothic romanticism of Nosferatu (1922) or Dracula (1931), Martin presents its titular character as a troubled young man who believes he's a vampire, using razor blades instead of fangs. The film's gritty Pittsburgh setting and documentary-style cinematography create an unsettling realism that makes its horror more immediate and disturbing than traditional vampire tales.

sections.content: Romero's decision to shoot Martin in a stark, naturalistic style influenced later psychological vampire films like Nadja (1994) and The Addiction (1995). The film's ambiguity about whether Martin is truly supernatural or mentally ill created a template for movies that blur the line between real and imagined horror, similar to The Transfiguration (2016) and A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night (2014).

Beyond its vampire elements, Martin serves as a powerful commentary on urban decay and generational conflict. The relationship between Martin and his elderly cousin Cuda mirrors Romero's exploration of social breakdown in Night of the Living Dead (1968) and Dawn of the Dead (1978), showing how horror can effectively address societal issues through genre conventions. sections.content: The film's influence extends into modern horror, with directors like Jim Jarmusch (Only Lovers Left Alive (2013)) and Ana Lily Amirpour acknowledging its impact on their work. Martin's complex character study approach to horror anticipated the current wave of "elevated horror" films like Raw (2016) and The Witch (2015), which prioritize psychological depth over conventional scares.
